cad: CAD models as Python, built by its engine (``cad.engine``) into documents and the files they
declare.

The root holds ``__version__``, ``CadDeprecationWarning`` and the document types, one object each
(``cad.registry``): ``model`` (a model built from code, held in the engine's memory, with no file), ``xbf``,
``step``, ``glb``, ``stl``, ``threemf``, ``dxf``, ``urdf``, ``sdf``, ``srdf``, ``kicad_pcb`` and
``kicad_sch``. A type is its decorator where it has one (``@model``, ``@step("arm.step")``), its edit where
its files are changed in place (``with kicad_pcb.edit("board.kicad_pcb") as board:``), its reader where it
has one (``step.read``) and its
operations, one to one with the ``cad <type> <operation>`` commands: ``.export`` and ``.snapshot``,
``.inspect``, and those named for what they do (``.dfm``, ``.solve``, ``.drc``, ``.erc``, ``.validate``). Our helpers that take build123d's objects are
the build123d integration's, ``cad.build123d`` (``memo``, ``paint``, the AP242 mechanism, a GLB's
``animation``, measurements, flat patterns); those that take trimesh's are the trimesh integration's,
``cad.trimesh`` (a mesh's 3D printing measurements: ``printing``, ``orientations``); those that call MuJoCo
are the mujoco integration's, ``cad.mujoco`` (a document as a ``mujoco.MjSpec``, a part's collision chosen on
it, the spec saved, and a MuJoCo model checked by MuJoCo's own compiler: ``spec``, ``fit``, ``save``, ``check``); those that take Blender's are the blender integration's, ``cad.blender`` (``load``: a
GLB in Blender's scene, for a render). Process control (``cad serve``, ``status``, ``stop``,
``server``) is the ``cad`` command's alone. Every name loads on first use: ``import cad`` imports no CAD
kernel, and ``import build123d`` binds a module the kernel loads into on its first attribute
(``_internal/lazy_kernel.py``). The earlier spellings (``cad.read_step``, ``cad.export``, ``cad.ap242``,
...) are aliases of what they name now, each saying so once (``_internal/aliases.py``).
The release of the library this is, as its distribution's metadata says it.

A spelling the library still answers, under the name it has now. A ``FutureWarning``, so Python
shows it by default: the people who read it are a model's authors, not a library's developers.

``cad.model``: the model document type, a model built from code and held in the engine's memory
(``cad.registry``).

A model has no file behind it: it is addressed by its document id (``cad run SCRIPT.py`` prints it) or
the handle its call returns. ``@model`` declares one (``@model(name=...)``; ``model(shape, name=...)`` hands
a shape over), with no file of its own; the files it declares are the other types' decorators
(``@xbf("XBF/arm.xbf")``, ``@step("arm.step")``). Its operations are the ``cad model <operation>`` commands':
``model.export(handle_or_id, *destinations, tolerance=None, angle=None)``, ``model.snapshot(...)``,
``model.inspect(...)`` and ``model.dfm(handle_or_id, process="cnc")`` (or ``"sheet"``, ``"molding"``,
``"printing"``), which checks it for manufacturing on its exact geometry, measured by the engine with the build123d
integration (``cad._internal.manufacturing``), and
``model.solve(handle_or_id, study=..., out="results/")``, a stress study of it (``cad._internal.fea.operation``),
which reads an ``.xbf`` the engine writes of it in a temporary folder. A file is
refused by name: ``arm.xbf`` is an xbf's (``cad.xbf``). Everything loads on first use: ``import cad.model``
imports no CAD kernel (``cad._internal.document_type``).

``@model`` or ``@model(name=...)``: declare a model; ``model(shape, name=...)``: hand a shape over as
a named model (``cad.engine.model.model``).

Write a document to each destination, its kind from its suffix (``.xbf``, ``.step``,
``.glb``, ``.stl``, ``.3mf``, ``.dxf`` of a planar document, and ``.xml`` or ``.mjcf``: an MJCF, the
document's robot description as MuJoCo reads one, its meshes in an ``assets`` folder beside it,
``export/mjcf.py``; ``.urdf``: the same description as ROS reads one, its meshes in a ``meshes``
folder beside it, ``export/urdf.py``): the document of an
``.xbf``, of a ``.step`` read into one, of a handle (``Document``) or a document id (the one the
engine holds, never built), or of a ``Model`` (called first, as this program's own call of it builds it); or a mesh file (``.glb``,
``.stl``, ``.3mf``) to the other two mesh kinds, each file holding what its format carries,
with no CAD kernel loaded (a mesh has no B-rep: no xbf, STEP, DXF, MJCF or URDF is made from one). Several
destinations read the document once. The file holds what the code built: no option selects a part or a state
(``README``, the law of options). ``daemon=False`` does it in this process, cold. A GLB
carries every configuration sequence the document defines, as a clip. A GLB, an STL and a 3MF are
meshed at the engine's one tolerance, the viewer's (a quarter per cent of each part and 28.5
degrees), unless ``tolerance`` gives an absolute ceiling in millimetres (at least
``export.MIN_TOLERANCE``), for a print whose fits are finer or a picture whose curves are, or
``angle`` a ceiling in degrees (``export.MIN_ANGLE`` to ``export.MAX_ANGLE``): each part is then
meshed again at the finer of each for these files, and each file says it; every destination is
then a GLB, an STL or a 3MF. An MJCF and a URDF are the robot description at the as-built state,
unless ``zero`` names a mechanism state to take every joint's zero at (``describe``'s **The zero**:
the bodies posed there, each joint's value there its zero, its limits and the other states around
it); every destination is then an MJCF or a URDF. Each robot file's ``Written.robot`` says what it
holds, and the program's own call says it on stderr after the file's line (``said.robot``). A call
the program's own
code makes (``python exports.py``) says each file, as ``cad <type> export`` does. Where the export is
goes, frame by frame, to ``progress`` (``progress.py``: its ``read`` of a file source, each
destination's ``write``), as ``_built`` takes it: by default a bar on stderr when it is a
terminal and nowhere when it is not, ``False`` nowhere, a callable each frame.

Draw a document (``.xbf``, ``.step``, or a document id: the one the engine holds) or a mesh
file (``.glb``, ``.stl``, ``.3mf``) into ``out`` (a ``.png``) as the viewer draws it: one
picture, a ``Drawn``. A ``Model`` is called first, as the program's own call of it builds it:
the document drawn is the one the engine then holds, whether or not an xbf of it is on disk. ``annotation`` (the viewer's
annotation: its file's path, its object, or the Quick Edit packet that carries it) and
``measurements`` are drawn over the model; ``camera="authored"`` draws it from the view the
annotation's ink was drawn in, which the packet holds. ``out`` a folder (a path ending in a
separator, or one that is there) is given a name inside it, the source's stem and the time
(``snapshot.picture_path``). A snapshot refused or failed leaves the file at ``out`` as it
was (``snapshot.write_png``). ``preview`` draws the viewer's Preview in place of a display mode: the
model lit in a studio, in its materials, on a floor with its shadow, in perspective.

``job`` in place of ``out`` is every picture a job names (``cad <type> snapshot --job``), a list of
``Drawn``: a Quick Edit packet (the ``.snapshot.json`` the viewer writes, its path or its
object), a job or a list of jobs, each job a view drawn as it was -- its camera, display, hidden
and isolated parts, pose, the packet's ink and dimensions -- at its output settings, into each
of its outputs (``snapshot.job_pictures``). ``source`` is then drawn in place of every job's
input; a flag given overrides every job. Every request is checked before anything renders, and
a picture that fails writes none of the job's, leaving every output as it was.

Where each picture is goes, frame by frame, to ``progress`` (``progress.py``: ``scene`` while the
document is served, meshed and its scene made, ``draw`` while the frame is drawn, ``write`` as
the picture is written), as ``export`` takes it: by default a bar on stderr when it is a
terminal and nowhere when it is not, ``False`` nowhere, a callable each frame.

What a ref names in a document (``refs``: ``hand/finger.2/face 7``, ``base/f:...``, a
copied ``/abs/kit.xbf#...`` line) and what made it. An element answers what the kernel
measures of it -- its points placed where its occurrence stands, in the document's frame --
with its canonical ``ref``, its occurrence's ``path`` and, of a model's document, ``made_by``
(a file names no model); a part or an assembly
its volume and its mass: each part's volume times its material's density, summed
(``cli.weighed``), its world bounds and a part's placement (``_placed``). One answer per selector (a list for several). Without ``ref``, the build
closure the xbf holds (``previous``): its engine, libraries, source, modules, inputs and
key, read from the file alone. A ref that names nothing, or several things, is refused by
name (``refs.RefError``). No query builds a missing model or writes its declared
outputs. ``query="build"`` returns file metadata/closure or live build metadata;
``query="geometry"`` requires a ref, and ``query="closure"`` accepts none.
``query="summary"`` (``cad xbf inspect DOC`` with no ref) is ``{"summary", "closure"}``:
what the document holds at a glance (``_summary``), and its closure, as the engine holds it; of
a GLB, ``{"mesh"}``: its nodes, meshes and animations, from its JSON alone (``_mesh``).
``query="structure"`` is the summary without bounds, volume or mass and requests no measurements.
No form meshes anything. A part's volume and box are cached by geometry key and measured in
batches. The summary's measurement goes, frame by frame, to ``progress`` (``progress.py``:
``inspect-measure``, ``measure``, counted as the engine tells each part's facts in), as ``export``
takes it -- by default a bar on stderr when it is a terminal and nowhere when it is not,
``False`` nowhere, a callable each frame.

Check a part for a manufacturing process: CNC machining, sheet metal, injection molding or 3D printing. Exit 0: OK. Exit 1: FAILED, a finding is an error (with --strict, a warning too). Exit 3: NOT CHECKED, something was not judged: never a pass. Exit 2: the command line's mistake.

A STEP, an xbf or a model's document is measured on its exact geometry, each finding at a face ref
(cad xbf inspect DOC REF resolves it). The measurements are facts; the verdicts are general rules, each
from a published design guide and no shop's limit, each finding coded by its rule, with the limit, the source
and what to change. A rule's feasibility limit broken is an error; a recommendation is a warning. For a named
shop, compare the measurements with its own published limits. --json carries every measurement, every rule's
outcome and each verdict as data (value, limit, unit, refs).
The last line and the exit status are the check's state. OK, exit 0: everything was measured and no
finding is an error. FAILED, exit 1: a finding is an error (with --strict, a warning too): the part cannot be
made by this process as drawn. NOT CHECKED, exit 3: the check did not judge what it was asked to -- a source
that does not read or holds no solid, a family that could not be measured, an engine that stopped -- which
is no verdict and never a pass. Exit 2: the command line's mistake.

source: a model's document id the engine holds (cad run SCRIPT.py prints it), or the handle its call returns.
process: cnc, sheet, molding or printing; default, for a STEP, an xbf or a model, the process the parts declare (part.material = metals.aluminum(process=machined()): machined is cnc, molded molding, fdm, sls, mjf, slm and vat printing with technology fdm, sls, mjf, pbf and sla), when every part agrees.
material: the part's material (aluminum, steel, stainless, abs, pc, nylon, ...): picks the material's limits; default the material the part declares (part.material = metals.aluminum()), when every part agrees.
axes: cnc: the milling machine's axes, 3, 4 or 5; default 3.
turning: cnc: the part is turned on a lathe (its axis found), not milled.
tools: cnc: the end mill diameters available, in mm, comma separated (3,6,10); default none: a corner is held to the smallest tool that can exist (0.05 mm across, text-to-cad's own floor) and to how deep a tool of its size reaches; a radius of 1.25 mm or more (a 2.5 mm end mill's) is recommended.
stock: cnc: the stock's size in mm (100x60x25); default the part's box.
thickness: sheet: the stock's thickness in mm; default measured.
k_factor: sheet: the neutral axis's place in the thickness, for the flat pattern (the shop's bend table's); default a K-factor chart's, by the material and each bend's radius.
bend_radius: sheet: the shop's inside bend radius in mm, compared with the part's.
kerf: sheet: the cutting kerf in mm, for small features.
sheet_size: sheet: the shop's largest sheet in mm (1219x2438); default a standard 5 x 10 ft sheet (3048x1524), assumed.
pull: molding: the pull direction, an axis (z, -y) or x,y,z components; default z.
wall_limit: molding: faces at or above this many degrees from the pull are not walls; default 45.
zero_tol: molding: draft under this many degrees is zero draft; default 0.05.
cavities: molding: cavities in the mold, for the clamp force; default 1.
technology: printing: fdm, sls, sla, mjf or pbf (metal powder bed); default fdm.
build_volume: printing: the printer's build volume in mm (256x256x256); default a typical machine of the technology's, assumed.
angle_limit: printing: down-facing faces under this many degrees from horizontal need support; default the technology's.
samples: printing: rays cast for the wall-thickness field on a mesh; default 2000.
layer_height: printing: the layer height in mm, for stair-stepping; default the technology's.
nozzle: printing: fdm's nozzle diameter in mm; default 0.4.
candidates: rank the candidates instead: molding the pulls (x, y, z and the part's principal axes), printing the orientations.
strict: a warning fails the check too (exit 1): a gate that takes no recommendation broken.

cad.model.interference: which parts of the document share volume.

Every pair of parts whose boxes meet is answered, as built and at each pose asked, in one of the engine's
checks processes: a pair whose meshes show air between the two parts shares nothing, and every other is measured
exactly by the kernel on the parts' own solids. Each answer is kept in the engine's cache by the two parts'
geometries and how one stands to the other, so a document edited is measured again only where a part that changed
is one of the two, and a check stopped by its time goes on from what it had measured. Nothing is built or
written, and the same check of an unchanged document is answered at once from the result the engine keeps: one
that answered every pair.

``poses``: the poses to check at beside as built, each a pose as every command takes one: a mechanism state's
name, a configuration sequence at a time of it (``"walk@0.6"``), or a ``{joint or coupling: value}`` table. The
check takes the poses it is given and chooses none: every state, or a sequence every tenth of a second, is the
caller's list. ``fits``: the pairs meant to share volume (a press-fit pin, a bearing in its bore), each two refs
or globs (``("pin", "base")``): listed apart, and no overlap. ``min_volume``: a shared volume at or below it
(mm3) is none; 0.001 by default, the rounding along a face where two parts touch.

Returns a ``cad.results.CheckResult``: ``ok`` when no two parts share volume and every pair was answered;
``failed`` with an ``overlapping_parts`` finding for each pair that does (``location`` and ``refs`` the two
occurrences' paths, ``value`` the most volume shared, mm3); ``not_checked`` (``reason``: ``unmeasured``)
when none was found but a pair could not be measured -- past its time, its process gone, the kernel's refusal --
which is never a pass: asked again, the check goes on from what it measured. ``measurements`` holds the poses,
the pairs counted (``pairs``: ``apart``, ``kept``, ``measured``) and every row (``overlaps``, ``fits``,
``unmeasured``: each ``between`` its two parts, with every pose it holds at). An option the document does not
answer -- a pose it has no state or sequence for, a fit that names nothing -- is refused by name (a
``ValueError``); a document that does not read is ``not_checked`` by its reason; a check that did not complete
raises as ``cad.engine.api.check`` says.

A linear static stress study of a part or an assembly bonded where its parts touch.

With no study it lists what a study names, writing nothing: the document's parts, the pairs that touch
(bonded by default) and one part's faces by ref with area, centre and a hint (`plane, normal -Z,
largest`). With a study and --out it meshes (netgen), solves (CalculiX, from cad[calculix]; CAD_CCX names
another) and writes its results into the folder --out names: result.json (every number, as --json prints
it), result.glb (the deformed surface coloured by stress, any viewer opens it), result.vtu (the volume's
fields, for meshio, PyVista or ParaView), stress.png and displacement.png (where a still can be drawn). Each
part's peak stress and safety factor against its own material's yield are in the result. A part that yields
or misses a check fails it, its results written all the same; a study whose answer would be wrong (a part
nothing holds, a load no face takes) is refused. --json carries every number.

source: the part or the assembly: a .step or .xbf, or a model's document id the engine holds (cad model
  solve), or the handle its call returns.
study: the study: a JSON file path, inline JSON, or (a library caller) a dict: the fixed faces, the
  loads (forces, pressures, gravity, acceleration), a material where the model has none, an
  assembly's parts and connections and the checks to judge. Without it, the setup.
out: the folder a solve writes its results into, made when missing; a study's alone.
occurrence: the part whose faces the setup lists, by its name or ref, where the document holds several.
deck: also write ccx.inp, the input CalculiX solved (the finer solve's when there were two); a study's alone.
verbose: say every progress line and the timings on stderr. Without it a long solve still says how far
  it has got about every 10 s.

Each joint's stops, found from the geometry: where its parts first meet another part.

Each joint a person moves is turned (or slid) alone from the as-built pose, the joints that follow it
with it and every other as built, a step at a time each way: a turn a full turn each way, a slide the
document's extent. Its stop each way is where its child link meets its parent link (each with what is
fixed to it): a stop whatever the other joints do, what its range declares. Where anything it moves
meets another link first, in the pose the others stand in, that clash is said beside the stop. Two parts
meet where they come within the clearance and within half their gap as built (less the 0.3 mm the
surfaces are sampled to), or where their contact grows by about 15 mm^2 on a surface that stops the motion:
parts touching already as built (a horn on its servo) meet only when their contact grows there or one is
pushed into the other (a part resting on its parent, turned into it, stops where it lies), parts near
as built (apart, within the clearance) only where their gap halves, and each joint's finding names them with
their gap as built and at each stop. A pair touching as built on a surface about the joint's axis (a plate
bolted to a motor's output, the output drawn as one solid with the motor's case) turns on it: neither that
face nor what of the output lies within its reach (a boss, a pin, a bolt's seat) stops the joint, and the
finding says the pair (turns on). A clash (anything the joint moves meeting another link, the other joints as
built) belongs to the drawn pose, which a simulator's contacts hold: the range is the stop. Parts drawn one inside the other (overlapping as built, a vendor's simplified parts sunk
into each other) meet only where one is pushed deeper into the other than drawn, by 0.6 mm more: each
joint's finding names them with the volume they share and how deep, and a stop they make lies past the
true one by up to about that depth. A larger clearance only narrows a range. Each joint's finding says its stops in degrees
or millimetres around the as-built pose (and in its own values where that is not zero) and which two
parts meet past each, every part tested against every other on its own surface. The model is not
changed: adopt the numbers into its joints' ranges. --json carries every number.

source: the document: a .step or .xbf, or a model's document id the engine holds (cad model ranges), or
  the handle its call returns.
step: the sweep's step: degrees for a turning joint, millimetres for a sliding one; default 1.
clearance: how near two parts' surfaces come before they count as touching, in millimetres; default 0.3,
  the least (where they all but touch): a larger one stops each joint where its parts first come that near.
joint: sweep this joint alone (repeat it for several); default every joint a person moves. A name the
  document has no such joint by is refused, naming its joints.
verbose: say on stderr each step as it starts (reading the document, sampling its surfaces, each joint)
  and each joint's stops as it ends (a joint or a sampling that takes long is said either way).

``cad.xbf``: the XBF document type, the engine's own document saved as a file (``cad.registry``).

``@xbf("XBF/arm.xbf")`` declares a model's XBF file;
``xbf.read(path)`` reads one into a model;
its operations (``xbf.export("arm.xbf", *destinations)``, ...) are the ``cad xbf <operation>`` commands',
each of an ``.xbf`` file: a model the engine holds, by its handle or id, is ``cad.model``'s.
``xbf.dfm(source, process="cnc")`` (or ``"sheet"``, ``"molding"``, ``"printing"``) checks it for manufacturing
on its exact geometry, with the build123d integration (``cad._internal.manufacturing``).
``xbf.solve(source, study=..., out="results/")`` runs a stress study on its part or bonded assembly, writing
its results into that folder (with no study, it lists the parts, pairs and faces a study names), with the
kernel, netgen and calculix integrations (``cad._internal.fea.operation``).
Everything loads on first use: ``import cad.xbf`` imports no CAD kernel (``cad._internal.document_type``).
Declare an explicit output: @xbf(out='path.xbf'), optionally named within the script folder by name=. The output path is required; decoration builds nothing.

An engine document (``.xbf``) as a build123d shape: a copy of its geometry, as
``read_step`` gives a STEP's -- a compound tree of its assembly, every part and group
named, coloured and given its materials (painted faces too) as the document has them,
each element named as the document names it. Its mechanism and configurations are not
imported: a part is a part. Read once per worker and held, keyed by the file's bytes, as
``read_step`` is. The fast way to bring a vendor STEP in: convert it once (``cadgen
export vendor.step vendor.xbf``) and read the xbf.

A ``.kicad_pcb`` is an AUTHORED file, edited in KiCad, as text or in place by :func:`edit`, never a
document a model makes: the type has no decorator. Its functions take paths and our own board objects, so
they are the type's, not the ``kicad`` integration's (the signature rule):

* :func:`read` parses the file and the ``.kicad_pro`` beside it with the standard library
  (:mod:`cad.engine.formats.kicad`), so a check script run with ``cad run`` imports it without the
  CAD kernel and without KiCad; :func:`inside` is the even-odd test a check measures a pour or an
  outline with, in the same millimetres.
* :func:`inspect` is the board in one look as plain data -- its format, thickness, size, layers, parts
  and nets -- what ``cad kicad_pcb inspect`` prints; ``snapshot`` draws it flat, as ``cad kicad_pcb
  snapshot`` does.
* :func:`edit` opens the saved board in KiCad's IPC API for a ``with`` block, the ``kicad`` integration's
  (``cad.kicad._session``): the block gets KiPy's open board, which is saved at its end when it was changed
  (made by KiCad when the file is not there yet) and not at all when the block raises.
* :func:`drc` (KiCad's design rule check) and :func:`export` (its fabrication, assembly and 3D outputs)
  run KiCad's own ``kicad-cli``, the ``kicad`` integration's (kicode, ``cad[kicad]``): they are the
  commands ``cad kicad_pcb drc`` and ``cad kicad_pcb export``, one to one. Where this environment lacks
  kicode, the command runs them in the environment of ``cad[kicad]`` the engine makes on first need; a
  function called here says to install the extra (or run the script with ``cad run``, which does).

The KiCad board at ``path`` (a ``.kicad_pcb``; any board KiCad opens) for board references.

Everything is in KiCad's frame: millimetres, y down, as the board file holds them. Reads
the file and the ``.kicad_pro`` beside it (for net classes); runs nothing.

KiCad's ``to`` export of the saved ``board`` into the folder ``out`` (``cad kicad_pcb export BOARD
--to KIND -o DIR``): ``to`` is one of ``gerbers``, ``drill``, ``pos``, ``bom``, ``step``, ``glb``,
``odb``, ``ipc2581``, ``pdf`` and ``dxf`` (``cad.kicad._export``'s table says what each writes). The
result says the files written and any warning. ``RuntimeError`` in KiCad's words when it fails.

What the board at ``path`` holds, as plain data: ``file``, ``format``, ``thickness``, ``size``,
``layers``, ``parts``, ``nets`` and ``counts`` (``cad kicad_pcb inspect``).

Check the KiCad board BOARD with KiCad's design rule check.

Runs ``kicad-cli pcb drc`` on the saved file with every severity reported
and lists each violation and unconnected item with where it is (millimetres
from the board's origin). The board fails when any error-severity violation
or any unconnected item exists; warnings are reported and do not fail it.
The result's ``measurements["drc"]`` is every finding as KiCad reported it,
each item with its uuid and position.

board: the .kicad_pcb to check (its .kicad_pro beside it carries the rules).

The board at ``board`` open in KiCad, for a ``with`` block: ``with kicad_pcb.edit("board.kicad_pcb") as
b:`` hands the block KiPy's open board (kicode's ``kicode.board.Board``), through kicode's headless
``kicad-cli api-server``. At the block's end the board is saved when it was changed (KiCad's own modified
state), so a block that changes nothing leaves the file byte for byte; when the block raises, nothing is
saved and the exception goes on. A board not there yet is made by KiCad, with its project, and saved. A
``kicad_sch.edit`` of the same project inside the block shares its KiCad. A saved board is checked for the
nets KiCad moved (it gives copper the net of a pad it overlaps): each track, via, copper shape or zone saved
on another net than the block gave it, else the file had, is a warning on stderr and, after the block, one
of ``b.net_changes`` (``kind``, ``id``, ``ref``, ``was``, ``now``, ``pad``, ``joined``). Needs the kicad extra
(``cad[kicad]``; ``cad run`` gives a script that calls it the extra).
Even-odd: KiCad's fills are single outlines with their holes cut in by slits.

``cad.kicad_sch``: the KiCad schematic document type (``cad.registry``), a saved KiCad schematic.

A ``.kicad_sch`` is an AUTHORED file, edited in KiCad, as text or in place by :func:`edit`, never a
document a model makes: the type has no decorator. A schematic is a hierarchy: its project's root sheet
(the ``<project>.kicad_sch`` beside the ``.kicad_pro``) and the sheets it places, each a file of its own.
Its functions take paths and plain values, so they are the type's, not the ``kicad`` integration's (the
signature rule):

* :func:`read` reads the whole hierarchy from the root, whichever of its sheets it is given,
  with the standard library (:mod:`cad.engine.formats.kicad.schematic`), so a script run with ``cad
  run`` imports it without the CAD kernel and without KiCad: its sheets, symbols and their pins,
  wires, labels and the nets they make, and ``resolve(ref)`` for a reference in the board's grammar
  (``#U3``, ``#U3.7``, ``#net:VBUS``) and the schematic's own (``#sheet:/Power/``, ``#wire:<uuid>``).
* :func:`inspect` is the schematic in one look as plain data -- its sheets, parts and nets, and what a
  reference names -- what ``cad kicad_sch inspect`` prints; ``snapshot`` draws one sheet flat, as
  ``cad kicad_sch snapshot`` does.
* :func:`edit` opens the saved schematic in KiCad's IPC API for a ``with`` block, the ``kicad``
  integration's (``cad.kicad._session``): its project's symbol libraries loaded, saved at the block's end
  when it was changed and not at all when the block raises.
* :func:`erc` (KiCad's electrical rules check) and :func:`export` (a pdf, svgs, the netlist, a BOM) run
  KiCad's own ``kicad-cli``, the ``kicad`` integration's (kicode, ``cad[kicad]``), as the board's do: they
  are the commands ``cad kicad_sch erc`` and ``cad kicad_sch export``, one to one. Where this environment
  lacks kicode, the command runs them in the environment of ``cad[kicad]`` the engine makes on first need;
  a function called here says to install the extra (or run the script with ``cad run``, which does).

The KiCad schematic at ``path`` (a ``.kicad_sch``: the root sheet or any sheet of its project's
hierarchy) for references: every sheet from the project's root down, its symbols and its nets.

Everything is in KiCad's frame: millimetres, y down, on each sheet's page. Reads the sheet files
alone; runs nothing.

KiCad's ``to`` export of the saved ``schematic``'s hierarchy into the folder ``out`` (``cad kicad_sch
export SCHEMATIC --to KIND -o DIR``): ``to`` is one of ``pdf`` (every sheet), ``svg`` (one a sheet),
``netlist`` (the one a board imports) and ``bom``. The result says the files written. ``RuntimeError``
in KiCad's words when it fails.

What the schematic at ``path`` holds, as plain data: ``file``, ``root``, ``format``, ``sheets``,
``parts``, ``nets`` and ``counts``; with ``ref``, ``resolved``: what that reference names
(``cad kicad_sch inspect``).

Check the KiCad schematic SCHEMATIC with KiCad's electrical rules check.

Runs ``kicad-cli sch erc`` on the saved hierarchy (from its project's root sheet) with every
severity reported, and lists each violation with its sheet and where it is (millimetres on that
sheet's page). Beside KiCad's, a warning for every pin joined some other way besides, and every wire's
end, that lies on a wire's span with no junction there (``pin_on_wire_span``, ``wire_end_on_wire_span``):
KiCad joins them and its ERC passes. A pin whose one connection is a wire's span is KiCad's own straight
run through a pin (it saves a rail drawn to each pin as one wire across them), not a finding. The schematic fails when any error-severity violation exists; warnings are reported and
do not fail it.

schematic: the .kicad_sch to check (any sheet of its project: the check reads the whole hierarchy).

The schematic at ``schematic`` (its project's root sheet, or any sheet) open in KiCad, for a ``with``
block: ``with kicad_sch.edit("design.kicad_sch") as s:`` hands the block KiPy's open schematic (kicode's
``kicode.schematic.Schematic``), through kicode's headless ``kicad-cli api-server``, its project's symbol
libraries (its own ``sym-lib-table``) loaded first; a placement from a library the project does not list
is refused in one line naming it. At the block's end the schematic is saved when it was changed, so a
block that changes nothing leaves the file byte for byte; when the block raises, nothing is saved and the
exception goes on. A schematic not there yet is made by KiCad, with its project, and saved. A
``kicad_pcb.edit`` of the same project inside the block shares its KiCad. Needs the kicad extra
(``cad[kicad]``; ``cad run`` gives a script that calls it the extra).

``cad.build123d``: the build123d integration -- our helpers that take build123d's objects.

build123d (and the OCCT kernel under it, OCP) is the integration model code builds with. Its extra
is ``cad[build123d]``; its code runs in the process that calls it. This namespace holds only what WE
define for it, never build123d itself (``import build123d as bd`` stays build123d's): the producers
that make the document types from a build123d shape (``_producers``, registered in ``cad.registry``),
and the helpers a model calls with build123d objects:

* ``memo``: a function worth replaying on a later build (the engine's **Memo functions**);
* ``paint(shape, faces, material)``: a material or colour on some faces;
* what a part declares for a robot description, each a fact of the machine:
  ``frame(part, name, location)``, a named frame in its own frame (a robot description's sites),
  ``body(part, name=)``, a body of its own fixed to its link, ``limits(assembly, joint, effort=,
  velocity=)``, a joint's drive limits, ``mass(shape, grams)``, what a part or an assembly weighs in
  all, ``point_mass(part, grams, at, name=, inertia=)``, a lump its solids leave out, ``free(shape)``, a
  base not bolted to the world, and ``link(shape, name)``, the name of the link its parts make;
* the mechanism, as ISO 10303-242 (AP242) names its entities: ``mechanism_state``
  (``mechanism_state_representation``), ``configuration_sequence``
  (``interpolated_configuration_sequence``), ``gear_pair``, ``rack_and_pinion_pair``, ``screw_pair``,
  and ``posed(assembly, state)``, a copy of the assembly at a state;
* ``animation(assembly, name, duration=)``: a glTF animation, baked into each GLB the model declares;
* measurements of native geometry: ``closest_points``, ``overlap_volume``, ``is_sound``,
  ``topology_errors``, ``boundary_edges``, ``self_intersections``, ``mass_properties`` and their
  result types;
* flat patterns, exact 2D geometry from a solid's planar faces: ``flat_pattern``, ``planar_faces``,
  ``flatten_face``, ``flatten_faces``, ``union_faces``, ``offset_profile``;
* ``leaves(tree)``: every leaf of a tree (``step.read``'s, ``xbf.read``'s, a model's ``.shape``) placed where
  it stands, out of the tree, on the same B-rep: what ``located`` gives without copying the tree;
* the manufacturing check of exact geometry, a ``CheckResult`` with its findings at refs (``plate/face 7``):
  ``dfm(shape, process=...)`` -- what ``cad.step.dfm`` and ``cad.xbf.dfm`` run on a file's or a document's
  B-rep (``_dfm_check``; the measurements ``_dfm_brep`` and ``_dfm_<process>``) -- with ``cnc``,
  ``sheet_metal``, ``molding`` and ``printing`` its four processes by name;
  and ``unfold(shape, k_factor=)``, a bent sheet's flat pattern, its bends unrolled by their bend allowance;
* ``materials``, a submodule: named looks for what bd_materials' catalogue lacks (solder mask, ENIG,
  moulding compound, anodized, powder coat, ...), each a native ``bd_materials.FinishedMaterial``.

Every name loads on first use: ``import cad.build123d`` imports no CAD kernel.
The kernel could not establish the requested geometric result.

Name an animation of an assembly: a GLB's own choreography, ``duration`` seconds long,
returned as a builder of glTF channels; its calls chain::

    show = animation(car, "showcase", duration=6)
    show.channel("lid", path="translation", keys=[(0, (0, 0, 0)), (1, (0, 0, 40))])
    show.rotation("wheel*", axis=(0, 1, 0), turns=3, start=1, interpolation="LINEAR")
    show.translation("door", by=(0, 300, 0), start=2, end=4)
    show.explode("body/*", radial=True, distance=40, end=2)       # helpers, compiled to channels
    show.hide("roof", at=3)                                       # a STEP scale channel to 0
    show.pose(at={0: "shut", 5: {"doors": 1}})                    # the mechanism, by its FK

``.channel(parts, path=, keys=, interpolation=)`` is glTF's channel (``path``
``translation``, ``rotation`` or ``scale``; ``interpolation`` ``CUBICSPLINE``, ``LINEAR`` or
``STEP``); ``.translation``, ``.rotation`` and ``.scale`` are channels from a start to an end.
Parts are named as a ref's owner names them (a label, ``hand/finger.2``), or by a glob
(``wheel*``). A configuration sequence is the mechanism's and the document keeps it; an animation is the GLB's:
never written into the xbf, baked into every GLB the model declares when that GLB is written.
Returns the builder.

Keep ``part`` a body of its own, rigidly fixed to the link it would have merged into, named
``name`` (the part's label where None): its mass, visuals, collision and frames go with it, not
into that link's. A part that is all of its link is a body already. A part's, not an
assembly's. Returns ``part``.

Free edges of a shell; seams are not boundaries.

An empty result establishes no free edges, not full manifold validity.
Geometry is neither sewn nor repaired.

Minimum set distance and one minimizing pair, in the input frame.

Solid interiors count: contact, overlap and containment have distance
zero. Witnesses need not be on both boundaries or unique. This is not
penetration depth. Pass faces/shells to ask about their boundaries.

Its cost grows with both shapes' faces (OCCT's exact extrema): two
solids of thousands of faces each (a vendor STEP's printed parts) take
seconds a pair, so a hundred pairs take minutes. Compounds are measured
member by member, a member whose bounding box is farther than the best
distance so far skipped. Over many pairs, rule out first those whose
``bounding_box(optimal=False)`` envelopes do not meet, and measure from a
point (``bd.Vertex``) where a point answers the question.
CNC machining's check of ``shape``: ``dfm(shape, process="cnc", ...)``.

Name a configuration sequence of an assembly's mechanism (AP242's
``interpolated_configuration_sequence``), by joint label: waypoints ``[(t, pose), ...]``
(``t`` in seconds from 0, ``pose`` a mechanism state's name or ``{joint: value}``, the rest
as built), ``sweep={joint: (from, to)}`` with ``duration``, or a function ``t -> {joint:
value}`` with ``duration``. ``ease`` is ``cubic`` (eased in and out at every waypoint:
AP242's synchronous interpolation) or ``linear``. A sequence is a finite clip; a player
repeats it::

    configuration_sequence(arm, "cycle", [(0, "folded"), (2, "reach"), (5, "folded")])
    configuration_sequence(arm, "wave", [(0, {"wrist": -30}), (1, {"wrist": 30}), (2, {"wrist": -30})])
    configuration_sequence(arm, "nod", lambda t: {"elbow": 45 + 20 * math.sin(t)}, duration=6)

The document keeps the definition, never frames (a function as its samples); a GLB
export bakes it into a clip of the same name, and STEP, STL and 3MF ignore it. It never
moves the build: the model is as its joints connect it. Returns ``assembly``.

The manufacturing check of a live build123d ``shape`` (a part, or an assembly's every part), as
``cad.step.dfm`` checks a file: ``process`` is ``cnc``, ``sheet``, ``molding`` or ``printing`` -- with
none, the one the parts declare (``part.material = metals.aluminum(process=machined())``) -- and the
options are that process's, by the names ``cad.step.dfm`` takes (``tools=[3, 6]``, ``pull="z"``,
``technology="sla"``); ``candidates`` ranks molding's pulls or printing's orientations instead, and
``strict`` fails the check on a warning too. A ``CheckResult``: its ``status`` (``ok``, ``failed``,
``not_checked``), its findings at refs (``plate/face 7``), each rule's verdict with its figure and its
limit, and its ``measurements``, the report. ``TypeError`` for an option no process takes.

Select, flatten, fuse, and optionally kerf-offset — the usual whole job.

The three steps are separately available above for drawings that need them
apart (a multi-plane bracket flattens each flange with its own selection
before one union).

Lay one planar face into the XY plane, exactly.

The face is moved by the rigid transform that takes its own plane to XY — no
sampling, no projection error, and every curve survives as itself. A DXF is
2D and the engine refuses geometry off the XY plane, so this (or an explicit
``bd.Location((0, 0, -z)) * face``) is how a derived face becomes drawable.

A face whose normal points away from +Z comes back mirrored, because that is
what looking at it from its own side means. Flip the source face first if you
want the other handedness.
:func:`flatten_face` over a selection.

Name a frame on ``part``: ``location`` (a build123d ``Location`` -- ``Pos``, ``Rot`` -- or a
``Plane``) in the part's own frame, the one its geometry is in before ``part.location``. A
second frame of one name replaces the first. A frame is a part's, not an assembly's: put it
on the part it stands on. Returns ``part``.

A gear train of ``assembly``'s mechanism, ``name``: revolute joints, by label, each turning
by its ratio (degrees per unit of the coupling's value) and only through it -- written as
AP242's ``gear_pair`` couplers, from the first-named joint to each other one. At value ``c``
each joint stands at its as-built angle plus its ratio times ``c``: ``c = 0`` is as built, so
it never moves the build. Its range is its joints' limits: the tightest interval in which each
stays within its own. Its name poses wherever a joint's does: ``mechanism_state(..., drive=90)``,
a configuration sequence's waypoints and sweeps, and ``--pose``; its joints alone are not posed.
A joint that is not revolute is refused when the document is made; a label names the joint
in each placement of a sub-assembly placed several times. Returns ``assembly``.

The boolean kernel's argument check (``BRepAlgoAPI_Check``) passes the
shape: BRepCheck-valid, no self-intersections, no too-small edges, and an
argument type a boolean accepts. This is what a fuse or cut demands of an
operand, and it can be expensive. A null or empty shape is not sound: the
kernel rejects it as an argument type (``BOPAlgo_BadType``), a verdict,
not an error. A check the kernel could not complete raises
``GeometryError``. Closure, solid count and signed volume are separate
questions; the faulty entities are ``self_intersections``'s.

Every leaf of ``tree`` (a node with no children), in tree order, placed in the tree's frame.

Each is a new shape of the leaf's own class, label, colour and material, detached from the tree (no
parent), its location the product of its ancestors' and its own: what ``leaf.located(world)`` gives,
without copying the tree. It shares its B-rep with the tree's leaf, so it costs no kernel copy however
large the assembly. ``paths=True`` gives ``(path, leaf)`` pairs instead, ``path`` the labels from the
root to the leaf (a label never given is ``""``), so a leaf is found by where it is in the assembly as
well as by its name.

Bound the drive of every revolute or linear joint labelled ``joint`` on ``assembly`` or below
it: ``effort`` in N*m for a revolute joint and N for a linear one, ``velocity`` in rad/s or m/s
(URDF's ``<limit effort velocity>``, MJCF's ``actuatorfrcrange``; MJCF bounds no speed), each
positive, each None where the model gives none. A cylindrical or a ball joint, of two and three
values, is refused. A second declaration for one joint replaces the first. Declare it after the
joint is made: it is kept on the part that holds it. Returns ``assembly``.

Name ``name`` the link the parts at or below ``shape`` make in a robot description, instead of
its first part's label: one link, so ``shape``'s parts must all be one link's, and no other link may
take the name (both refused when the robot is described). A part declared a body is named by its
``body`` declaration. A second declaration replaces the first. Returns ``shape``.

Say that ``shape``, a part or an assembly, weighs ``grams`` in all, its point masses included:
its solids keep their densities' ratios and are scaled alike to make up the rest (the module's
**Mass**, where nested declarations are). A second declaration replaces the first. Returns
``shape``.

Add uniform-density solids, including overlapping material as supplied.

Density must be finite and positive, in mass/input-unit³. Inertia is
about the combined center of mass, expressed in the input coordinate
axes. For mm and kg/mm³ the outputs are mm³, kg, mm and kg·mm².

``cad.build123d.materials``: named looks for what bd_materials' catalogue lacks.

Printed circuit boards and their parts, and the common process finishes, as scalar looks that the
viewer, an OCCT still and a GLB all draw (no texture maps: a part's mesh has no UVs)::

    from cad.build123d import materials

    board.material = materials.soldermask("green")
    paint(board, pads, materials.enig())
    housing.material = materials.anodized("black")
    bracket.material = materials.powder_coat("RAL7016", finish="satin")

Each factory returns a fresh native ``bd_materials.FinishedMaterial``: the physics one of bd_materials' own
classes (its metals' and FR-4's tables where they have them, renamed for the look; ``custom_metal`` and
``custom_plastic`` or ``SolidMaterial`` where they do not), the look a ``threejs_materials.PbrProperties``.
No class of its own, so any release that reads an xbf reads these. A ``color`` is a preset name, an sRGB
hex string, a CSS name or an sRGB (r, g, b) of 0-1 floats; ``zinc_plated`` takes its passivation instead,
one of four. One finish is one material, named once whichever spelling asked for it: a preset by any of
its names, or by its hex, is that preset (named by its first name in the table), and any other colour is
named by its sRGB hex, so two parts of one look are one row of a BOM. ``substrate=`` takes the
bd_materials metal a finish is on; its physics are kept, its look replaced.

Nothing here loads before a factory is called: ``import cad.build123d.materials`` imports neither
bd_materials nor threejs_materials.

A board in solder mask over FR-4 (its physics bd_materials' FR-4): ``glossy`` a clear-coated
lacquer, ``matte`` a flat one. Presets: green, black, blue, red, white, yellow, purple.
The common board: glossy green solder mask over FR-4.
Matte black solder mask over FR-4.
Bare FR-4 laminate, unmasked: a pale yellow-green glass-epoxy (a board's edge, a slot's wall).

Silkscreen ink, flat and matte, painted on a board's faces. Presets: white, black, yellow.
An ink has no bulk physics: its density is unknown.
Bare copper (bd_materials' C110), bright, or ``oxidized`` to a dull brown-orange.

ENIG (electroless nickel, immersion gold) on copper pads: a pale, slightly satin gold. The physics
are the pad's copper; the plating is microns thick.

HASL (hot-air solder levelled) tin on copper pads: bright, the lead-free alloy a little duller.
The physics are the pad's copper.
Solder (SAC305, Sn-3Ag-0.5Cu): a joint, a fillet, a ball. Its own physics (``custom_metal``).

Black epoxy moulding compound: an IC package, a moulded module. Its own physics (``custom_plastic``,
silica-filled epoxy).

A ceramic body: a chip capacitor's (``tan``), a resistor's or a substrate's (``white``). Physics:
96% alumina (``SolidMaterial``). Presets: white, tan, beige.

An LED's lens, clear epoxy that light passes through (``transmission``), tinted by ``color``;
``diffused`` a frosted one. Presets: clear, white, red, green, blue, amber, yellow. The tint is the
base colour alone, which tints the light a transmissive look passes (three.js, glTF) and is the
colour a look without transmission draws: an attenuation colour as well would tint it twice, the
lens far darker than its colour, and more so the thicker the part.

A connector's or a switch's housing: glass-filled PBT (PBT-GF30, ``custom_plastic``), moulded
satin. Presets: black, white, natural, beige, grey.

Anodized aluminium (bd_materials' 6061-T6 unless ``substrate``): the dyed oxide over the metal,
satin. Light passes the dyed oxide to the metal and back, so a dyed part reflects its surroundings
in its dye's colour: drawn as a mostly metallic surface of that colour (metalness 0.7), clear (and
silver) as nearly the bare metal (0.9), black as a deep dye that reflects less (0.45), each under a
light clear coat, the oxide's sheen. Presets: clear, silver, black, grey, red, blue, gold, green,
purple, orange.
Black anodized 6061-T6.

Powder coat over a metal (bd_materials' mild steel unless ``substrate``): an opaque polymer skin,
``matte``, ``satin`` or ``gloss``. Presets: RAL9005, RAL9010, RAL9016, RAL7016, RAL7035, RAL7024,
RAL3020, RAL5010, RAL1023, RAL6005, and black, white (RAL9016) and grey (RAL7016).
Satin black powder coat on mild steel.

Bead-blasted metal (bd_materials' 6061-T6 unless ``substrate``): an even, diffuse satin in the
bare metal's own colour (bd_materials' look of its family), whatever finish the substrate wore.

Brushed metal (bd_materials' 304 stainless unless ``substrate``): satin, its highlight stretched
across the grain (``anisotropy``), the grain around the part's Z axis.

Zinc-plated steel (bd_materials' mild steel unless ``substrate``), passivated ``clear``, ``blue``,
``yellow`` or ``black``. Each passivation is its own chemistry, its colour, metalness and roughness
together, so it takes one of those four, not a colour.

Black-oxide steel (bd_materials' mild steel unless ``substrate``): a dark, faintly metallic
conversion coat, ``oiled`` a little glossier.

Name a state of an assembly's mechanism (AP242's ``mechanism_state_representation``):
``mechanism_state(arm, "raised", elbow=90)`` sets the joint labelled ``elbow`` to 90
degrees in the state ``raised`` (a number per joint, or for a joint of several values a
sequence: a cylindrical joint's angle and position, a ball joint's three angles). The
joints are build123d's, placed with ``connect_to``; the values they were connected at are
the as-built state, and a joint a mechanism state does not name stays as built. The
document keeps every mechanism state; the viewer offers them as presets, ``--pose NAME``
draws a snapshot at one, and a configuration sequence's waypoint may name
one. A mechanism state never changes the build: every file shows the model as built. A
value outside its joint's range fails the build, in one line naming the state, the joint,
the value and the range; one on a bound is within it. Returns ``assembly``.

Mark a function worth replaying: ``@memo``, bare. Its arguments are keyed by value
(plain values, build123d's value types, materials, shapes the engine made); it returns
geometry (a shape, or a tuple, list or dict of shapes); it writes nothing outside
itself. A verifying build (``Model.build(verify=True)``)
runs every call the engine would replay and compares what it makes with what was logged.
Injection molding's check of ``shape``: ``dfm(shape, process="molding", ...)``.

Kerf / tool-radius compensation, exactly.

Positive grows the profile (cut outside the line), negative shrinks it (cut
inside). The offset is OCC's, so a filleted corner offsets to a concentric
arc rather than to a fan of chords — the single biggest reason this module
stopped going through shapely.

Intersection volume of two finite, positively oriented solids, or of
compounds of them: an assembly's leaf part is often a Compound.

A compound is its solids, each placed as the compound places it, and the
answer is the sum of every pair's overlap (one solid of ``a``, one of
``b``): solids of one compound that overlap each other count their shared
region once per solid, and are never fused. Contact has zero volume.
Assembly pair selection, intentional overlaps and acceptance thresholds
belong to the caller. Inputs are never fused or modified; a failed boolean
is an error, never a zero-volume answer.

Colour faces of a part, or give them a material: ``faces`` (a face, or several) of
``shape`` take ``color`` -- an sRGB hex string (``"#e68019"``, ``"#e68019cc"``), 0-255
integers (three, or four with alpha), a build123d ``Color``, or a ``bd_materials.FinishedMaterial`` -- in the
document, by their ordinal in the part. The colour is the one ``shape.color`` would give
the same value (``colors``). A face holds one paint: a colour
replaces its material, a material its colour. Returns ``shape``, whose paints the
memo keys like its label.

A part's material is set as its colour is, on the shape: ``part.material =
bd_materials.metals.mild_steel()``; on an assembly, it is every part's below it that has none. Both
are attributes of the object, and travel as build123d moves them: a copy, ``moved``
and ``located`` keep them. Material assignment uses build123d's native property;
set an explicit colour after assigning a material to override its PBR base colour.
Paint and materials are for finished parts: set them after the last
operation, so an edit of one is no kernel call (the memo keys them with the shape,
and a compound does not hold its children's materials in its key).

The planar faces of ``shape`` facing one way at one height.

This is the selection step of a flat pattern: "every upward face of the top
surface", "every outward face of the left flange". Raises rather than
returning nothing — an empty selection means the plane or the sign is wrong,
and a drawing generated from no faces is an empty file nobody notices.

Add ``grams`` to ``part`` at ``at`` (a build123d ``Location`` or ``Plane``) in its own frame, the
one its geometry is in before ``part.location``, as a frame is: a lump its solids leave out. It has
no inertia of its own unless ``inertia`` gives its diagonal, ``(ixx, iyy, izz)`` in kg*m^2 about
the point in ``at``'s axes. ``name`` tells several apart (``point1``, ``point2`` where None); a
second of one name replaces the first. A part's, not an assembly's. Returns ``part``.

``assembly`` with every part where ``state`` puts it: a mechanism state's name, or
``{joint label or coupling name: value}`` (the values ``mechanism_state`` takes, the rest as
built). The parts move by the forward kinematics the viewer and the snapshot use
(``link_worlds``): each link's placement at the asked values over its placement as built,
applied to that link's parts. An unknown state, joint or coupling, or a value out of range, is
refused by name (``resolve``).

``assembly`` is what the model call returned, its document's handle, or a shape. Inside a body
(``return posed(arm(), "folded")``: a posed file is this) the result is a copy of the shape that
shares its geometry and keeps the joints, couplings, mechanism states and configuration
sequences, the asked values its as-built state; a value a state or a sequence gives a coupling
is said again from that state (``_rebase``), so each names the pose it named. From a plain script (a check) the handle's
document is posed where the engine holds its mechanism (``posed_structure``), and the answer is
the tree ``.shape`` is, at that pose: placed parts, no joints. A shape a plain script read
through ``.shape`` has no joints left to pose, and is refused with what to pass instead.
3D printing's check of ``shape``: ``dfm(shape, process="printing", ...)``.

A rack and pinion of ``assembly``'s mechanism, ``name``: the first-named joint, by label,
on one side -- a revolute joint (the pinion) or a prismatic one (the rack) -- and every other
joint of the other kind, each moving by its ratio (degrees or millimetres per unit of the
coupling's value) and only through it; written as AP242's ``rack_and_pinion_pair`` couplers,
from the first-named joint to each other one. Its value, range and naming are a gear pair's
(``gear_pair``). A joint of the wrong kind is refused when the document is made.

The pinion may hold no part: a ``RevoluteJoint`` on the part that carries it, connected to
nothing, is a **virtual pinion** -- a reference axis where the CAD draws no gear, so two slides
couple to each other through it (``rack_and_pinion_pair(gripper, "grip", pinion=1, left=0.15,
right=0.15)``, its ratios the pitch circle's millimetres per degree). The document keeps it as a
revolute pair to a link of no part; a robot description writes the racks coupled to the first of
them and no pinion. Give it a range at least as wide as the racks' (build123d's default is 0 to
360): it bounds the coupling. Returns ``assembly``.

A screw of ``assembly``'s mechanism, ``name``: one cylindrical joint, by label, given its
pitch, ``lead=1.5`` (the millimetres it travels per 360 degrees of turn, negative for a left
hand) -- Part 105's ``SCREW_PAIR``, which holds the pitch and nothing else. The coupling's value
is the joint's turn from as built, in degrees; its travel follows. Its range and naming are a
gear pair's (``gear_pair``). A joint that is not cylindrical is refused when the document is
made. Returns ``assembly``.

Explicit boolean self-intersection check in the supplied placement.

This can be expensive. Codes are OCCT's ``BOPAlgo_SelfIntersect``; affected
entities are owned copies. Inconclusive/failed checks raise an exception.
Sheet metal's check of ``shape``: ``dfm(shape, process="sheet", ...)``.

BRepCheck topology/geometry faults, with affected owned entities.

Codes are OCCT's ``BRepCheck_*`` status names. Open shells and reversed
solids can have valid topology. Closure, signed volume and expensive
boolean self-intersection testing are separate questions.

The flat pattern of a bent sheet metal part (a build123d ``Shape``): exact 2D geometry in the XY
plane, ready to return from a ``@dxf`` model.

Each flange is rotated flat about its bend and the bend replaced by a strip as wide as its bend
allowance, ``BA = angle * (inside radius + K * thickness)``; holes and arcs stay exact. ``thickness``
(mm) is checked against the part's measured one; ``k_factor`` is the neutral axis's place in the
thickness (the shop's, from its bend table; default Hubs's air-bending chart by ``material`` and each
bend's radius). One part gives its flat ``Face`` (or a ``Compound`` of the
pieces that do not join); several parts, a ``Compound`` of each one's. With ``bend_lines`` the result
is a ``Compound`` of the cut outline labelled ``CUT`` and the bends' centre lines labelled ``BEND`` (an
empty one for a flat plate, which has none): a DXF writes each label as its own layer. ``ValueError`` for a
shape that is not one thickness of sheet.

Fuse coplanar XY faces into one profile, exactly.

OCC's boolean is the primary path: overlapping faces merge, shared edges
disappear, holes survive as inner wires, and arcs stay arcs. Disjoint faces
come back as a multi-face result, which is a perfectly good nested cut
layout.

Shapely is the fallback, and only that. OCC refuses some genuinely
degenerate inputs — faces that touch along a zero-width sliver, self-
intersecting projections of a fold — where a tolerant polygon union still
gives a usable contour. Taking that route costs curvature (the rebuilt
profile is polygonal), so it is never the default and never silent.

``cad.kicad``: the kicad integration -- our code for KiCad: kicad-cli and its IPC API, both kicode's.

KiCad's command line, ``kicad-cli``, is an external program our code runs (kind C), with a separate
process; its extra, ``cad[kicad]``, is kicode, which carries that program and KiPy, the IPC API's Python
client (as ``kicode``), one KiCad nightly's build of both. A person's own KiCad is never run. What is here:

* ``_program``: ``kicad-cli`` found and run, by the library's one helper for external programs
  (``cad._internal.programs``): ``CAD_KICAD_CLI``, refused unless it names a ``kicad-cli``, then
  kicode's; only ``kicad-cli`` itself is ever run, headless, in private homes (``kicode.environment``).
* ``_command``: ``cad run kicad-cli ARGS`` -- KiCad's own command line, the environment's (kicode's console
  script), headless in a private folder, its exit code kicad-cli's.
* ``_session``: what ``kicad_pcb.edit`` and ``kicad_sch.edit`` run, a ``with`` block -- a private
  ``kicad-cli api-server`` on the file (KiCad makes one not there yet), one per project, which the board's
  and the schematic's edits share; KiPy connected to it, the open document handed over (a schematic's
  project symbol libraries loaded first), saved at the block's end when it was changed and not when the
  block raises, the server stopped and its folder removed; ``_drift``, the board's check at the save of the
  nets KiCad moved onto a pad's.
* ``_check``: KiCad's design rule check (``cad.kicad_pcb.drc``, ``cad kicad_pcb drc``).
* ``_export``: the board's fabrication, assembly and 3D outputs by ``kicad-cli`` (``EXPORTS``: gerbers,
  drill, pos, bom, step, glb, odb, ipc2581, pdf, dxf), which ``cad.kicad_pcb.export`` and the server's ``cad
  kicad_pcb export`` are written by.
* ``_schematic``: a schematic's electrical rules check and its outputs (``EXPORTS``: pdf, svg, netlist,
  bom) by ``kicad-cli``, from its project's root sheet (``cad.kicad_sch.erc`` and ``export``, ``cad
  kicad_sch erc`` and ``export``).
* ``route`` (``_route``, its search in ``_routing``): copper for the connections an agent names, in the order
  it names them, written into the board a ``kicad_pcb.edit`` block has open: KiPy's board in, the copper out
  through it, every rule the board's own; it answers a ``Routed``.

The board readers are the document type's (``cad.kicad_pcb``), our own code for the file format: viewing,
reading and drawing a board need no KiCad. Importing this package starts nothing and imports no kicode.

What a ``route`` call did: every connection it was asked for, in the order routed (``connections``: each
its net, its two ends, routed or not and why not, the copper it added, the plan entry it came from), and the
totals. ``ok`` when every one is routed. ``warnings``: each custom rule the router does not keep (it holds where
a condition only KiCad's DRC evaluates, or is of a kind the router does not route by), and a plan whose region
was narrowed to fit the router's memory, said on stderr before routing too: DRC judges the rules after.
One line per warning, one per connection, then the totals.

Route ``connections`` in the board an edit has open (``with kicad_pcb.edit(path) as board``), in the order
given; see the module's doc. Each connection is a net (``"/CLK"``, ``"#net:/CLK"``), a pair of pads
(``("U1.3", "C4.1")``) or a dict of either with options; the keyword options apply to every entry that does
not set its own:

- ``layers`` (required, here or in each entry): the copper layers it may use, a list, or a mapping of each to
  its cost per millimetre (1 where a list names it);
- ``width``: the track's, mm (default: the net's netclass track width);
- ``clearance``: what it keeps from other nets, mm (default, and least: what DRC holds the net to);
- ``vias``: the most vias each entry may place, all its connections together (default: no limit; 0 for none);
- ``via_cost``: what a via costs, in mm of track (default 2); the search settles for a path within 1.2 times the
  cheapest, so it trades a via for track at about that cost, not exactly.

The board's custom rules (its ``.kicad_dru``) are kept as ``cad.kicad._routing.rules`` says: each clearance
everywhere, each size a rule holds everywhere at the entry (a track's width refused outside it, the via taken up
to it, a net's via count lowering the entry's via limit), a ``disallow`` or ``assertion`` refused; every other
one that can bear on new copper is a warning naming the rule, on stderr (``route: warning: ...``) before routing.

Answers a ``Routed``: each connection's outcome; ``.ok``, ``.failed``, ``.warnings``, ``.human_lines()``. A
connection that cannot be routed is said on stderr too. ``ValueError`` for a plan or a board it cannot route by, before anything is
routed (see the module's doc); ``TypeError`` for a board no edit has open.

``cad.trimesh``: the trimesh integration -- our measurements of a triangle mesh for 3D printing,
taking trimesh's ``Trimesh`` (its extra, ``cad[trimesh]``: trimesh, with rtree for its closest points,
scipy for its connected bodies and networkx for filling the face a body shares with another; the rays are
the library's own, in bounded memory).

Each returns the report as plain data, every figure in millimetres, degrees and square millimetres --
facts, never verdicts: nothing here compares a figure against a process's limit:

- ``printing(mesh)``: 3D printing -- the mesh, its scale, overhangs, wall thickness (ray cast, per body)
  and an estimate of the support volume;
- ``orientations(mesh)``: support area and build height for six axis-aligned orientations.

A family that cannot be measured leaves ``{"error": ...}`` where its facts would be, and the report
says so (``partial``, ``partial_sections``). The mesh is never changed: each measures a copy, scaled
by ``units`` to millimetres and cleaned as a file's mesh is (``_mesh``: welded, its collapsed triangles and
doubled slivers and zero-area debris dropped, its tessellation's cracks closed; watertightness judged per
body) and put through the same gate: a mesh with no inside to measure -- no triangles, a corner that is no
number, more than two million triangles, a one-sided surface, a closed one of no volume -- raises
``cad._internal.dfm.Unmeasured`` (its ``code`` and ``message`` the check's one finding), and what the gate
repaired is in the report's ``mesh``.

Injection molding is judged on exact geometry alone (a mesh's chords misread its draft, undercuts and walls):
check the part's STEP or model. A file is measured by its document type's check -- ``cad.stl.dfm("part.stl")``,
``cad.xbf.dfm(model_handle, process="printing")`` -- which answers a ``CheckResult`` whose
``measurements`` is this report and whose findings say what it shows (``cad <type> dfm --process``).
Everything loads on first use: ``import cad.trimesh`` imports no trimesh.
``printing``'s support area and build height for six axis-aligned orientations of ``mesh``.

3D printing's measurements of ``mesh`` (a ``trimesh.Trimesh``) as it stands on the plate (its
lowest point): overhangs and support counted for down-facing faces under ``angle_limit`` degrees from
horizontal, wall thickness from ``samples`` rays.

``cad.mujoco``: the mujoco integration -- our code that calls MuJoCo, taking its objects (its extra,
``cad[mujoco]``: ``mujoco-core``, the compiler and the Python bindings, numpy their one dependency, and
``mujoco-studio``, MuJoCo Studio's web viewer; no window system).

An MJCF is MuJoCo's own file and no document type: cad writes one and asks MuJoCo about one, and never
reads or shows one itself. ``check`` compiles a model with MuJoCo's own compiler and answers a check's result
-- what MuJoCo refused or warned of, in its words, the model-health checks, what the model collides as and
its contact excludes (``_check``; ``cad mujoco check FILE`` is its command, the integration's one operation
in ``cad.registry``). ``compile_model`` and ``compile_findings`` are the compile alone. ``cad run
mujoco-studio --model FILE`` shows the person a model in Studio's web viewer (``_command``: the environment's
own ``mujoco-studio``).

What it does for every document: ``spec`` makes one a ``mujoco.MjSpec`` (``_spec``): a model call's
handle, a build123d shape, a STEP or an xbf described as a robot and written as the engine's MJCF
export writes it (``cad.engine.export.mjcf``), for a scene to attach; an MJCF path read as it is.

What it does for a MuJoCo function -- a plain function that makes a robot's spec with ``spec``, makes the
simulator's choices on it in MuJoCo's own API and returns it: ``parts`` lists the spec's parts by label path,
and ``collisions``, ``fit`` and ``decompose`` find and replace one part's collision geoms by it (``_parts``: ``fit`` the kernel's primitive
of the part's exact solid, ``decompose`` CoACD's convex hulls of its mesh), and ``save`` writes the spec as a
folder that travels, by MuJoCo's own writer (``_save``).

Everything loads on first use: ``import cad.mujoco`` imports no mujoco. A helper called where the
extra is missing says so by name (``cad[mujoco]``), as every integration's does.

Compile one MuJoCo model with MuJoCo and check it.

MuJoCo's own compiler reads the model, so what it refuses or warns of is said in its words. Then
the model-health checks of MuJoCo's modelling guide run on the compiled model, and two facts are
said of it: what collides as what, body by body, and each contact exclude with how its two bodies
stand at rest (every geom and exclude a row of the result's measurements). Errors always block;
under ``strict`` warnings do too.

path: the .xml or .mjcf file to check.
strict: treat warnings as blocking.
verbose: narrate the target on stderr.

The collision geoms (``mujoco.MjsGeom``) of the part ``part`` names in ``spec`` (a spec ``spec`` made): its
label path, as ``cad model inspect`` prints it, a last segment enough where only one part ends in it; a list,
empty for a part that collides as nothing. A label that names no part, or two, is refused by name
(``cad.mujoco._parts``).

Compile the MJCF at ``path`` with MuJoCo and answer findings (``cad._internal.findings.FindingsReport``):
an error with MuJoCo's words for a model it refuses, a warning for each compile warning, an info saying the
compile passed or was skipped (``mode`` ``auto``, mujoco not installed here); ``required`` without mujoco
is an error naming the extra.

The model at ``path`` compiled by MuJoCo (``mujoco.MjModel``), its compile warnings beside it, as
``(model, warnings)``; MuJoCo's ``ValueError`` for a model it refuses.

Replace the collision of the part ``part`` names in ``spec`` with the convex hulls CoACD cuts its mesh into
(``cad[coacd]``): ``max_hulls`` at most that many (None for no limit), ``threshold`` CoACD's concavity
threshold, 0.01 to 1 (its 0.05 where None). Works on a spec read from an MJCF too. Its collision geoms.

Replace the collision of the part ``part`` names in ``spec`` with the primitive ``kind`` (``box``, ``sphere``,
``cylinder``, ``capsule``) the kernel fits to its exact solid (``cad.engine.describe.fit``); refused on a spec
read from an MJCF (no solids) and for a part read from a mesh. Its collision geoms.

The label paths of every part of ``spec`` (a spec ``spec`` made), sorted: the names ``collisions``, ``fit``
and ``decompose`` take. A spec read from an MJCF answers its colliding meshes' names (``cad.mujoco._parts``).

Write ``spec`` (a ``mujoco.MjSpec``) to ``path`` by MuJoCo's own writer, every file it names copied into
``assets/`` beside it, a ``scene.xml`` beside it where there is none and the spec has no floor of its own (no
plane geom on its world body: a scene gets none); the spec handed in is left as it was.
Prints the check's warnings, what the model collides as, its contact excludes and ``wrote <path>``; the
path written (``cad.mujoco._save``).

``thing`` -- a model call's handle, a build123d shape, a ``.step``/``.xbf`` path, or an MJCF path read as
it is -- as a ``mujoco.MjSpec`` for a scene to attach (``scene.attach(spec(arm()), prefix="arm/",
frame=...)``). Its meshes are written where MuJoCo will read them when the scene compiles: ``assets``, a
folder relative to the working directory where the scene is saved, else a folder of the engine's cache named
by what it holds (``cad.mujoco._spec``). ``tolerance`` meshes them to within it, in mm. ``zero``, a mechanism
state's name, takes a document's robot there, every joint's zero at that state, as an export's ``--zero`` does
(an MJCF's zero is its own, and a zero is refused).

``cad.coacd``: the coacd integration -- our code that calls CoACD, the approximate convex decomposition of a
triangle mesh (its extra, ``cad[coacd]``: the ``coacd`` wheel, numpy its one dependency, MIT).

What it does for a MuJoCo function: ``cad.mujoco.decompose(spec, part)`` makes a part collide as the convex
hulls CoACD cuts its mesh into, while its visual stays whole. The decomposer
(``_decomposer``) always runs in a process of its own, started by the engine (``cad.engine.hulls``, which keeps
the hulls in its cache by the mesh's digest and the options): CoACD's library carries a threading runtime (TBB)
of its own beside the kernel's, prints from native code and can die on a mesh it cannot repair, none of which
may reach the process that holds the kernel. Nothing of the tool is re-exported, and ``import cad.coacd``
imports no coacd.

cad's support for netgen, the mesher a stress study runs: always in a process of its own (:mod:`._mesher`). What
the mesh means is ``cad._internal.fea``'s. Nothing of the tool is re-exported.

cad's support for CalculiX, the solver a stress study runs: its ``ccx``, the cad-ccx package's (``cad[calculix]``), found,
checked and run headless (:mod:`._program`; ``cad run ccx``, :mod:`._command`), and its input and printed output
(:mod:`._files`). What the study means is
``cad._internal.fea``'s. Nothing of the tool is re-exported.

``cad.blender``: the blender integration -- a GLB loaded into Blender's scene for a render, taking and
answering Blender's own objects (its extra, ``cad[blender]``: bpy, Blender as a Python module, which has
builds for Python 3.13 alone).

    from cad.blender import load

    model = load("scene.glb", clip="explode", fps=24)
    model.root, model.box, model.clips      # the root's object, the world box in metres, each clip
    model.objects["arm/head/pin_1"]         # a node's object, by the node's name
    model.play("cycle")                     # another clip; model.play(None) stands still

``load`` imports the file with Blender's own glTF importer and answers a ``Model``: each node's object, the
clips, and the box of the pose the file was written in. It sets the scene's frame rate first (``fps``, with
``render.fps_base`` 1), which keys the clips' seconds. It undoes what that importer gets wrong with a file
that has clips: it leaves a node a clip moves at its first clip's start, so a still shows a pose the file
never held, with no error; only that first clip plays, and clearing it leaves its last pose; and it keys
every clip from frame 0, wherever the scene's range starts. Here every node a clip moves stands where the
file places it, and a clip plays alone (``Model.play``), the scene's range set to its frames, 0 to its
duration.

It opens any GLB, cad's or another tool's (build123d's ``export_gltf``, KiCad's board): a node is known by
its place in the file, never by the name Blender gives its object, so a node with no name, two of one name
and a name Blender cuts short are each found. A skin's joints are no objects but bones, of the armature Blender
makes for the skin (the skinned mesh's parent), found there by name; ``load`` places objects, never a bone.

Everything loads on first use: ``import cad.blender`` imports no bpy, and a script whose environment lacks it
is told which extra brings it. Nothing of Blender's is re-exported: ``import bpy`` stays Blender's.

One of the GLB's animations: ``kind`` is ``motion`` (a configuration sequence) or ``animation`` (an
``animation()``), empty for a file cad did not write; ``duration`` in seconds.

The imported model. ``root`` is the object of the scene's first root node (``roots``: of each, in the
file's order; for a root that is a skin's joint, the objects nearest it below). ``objects`` is each node's
object by the node's name (in a GLB cad wrote, its path below the root, ``arm/head/pin_1``); a node with
no name by the name Blender gave its object (``Mesh_0``, ``Node_3``); a name given twice, the last.
``nodes`` is each by its index in the file, which tells two of one name apart. Both hold every node
Blender made an object of: a skin's joints are bones (the module). ``clips`` by name, ``box`` the world
box (low, high corners in metres) of the pose the file was written in, ``fps`` the scene's frame rate
(``fps_base`` 1), and ``clip`` the one playing.

Play the clip ``name`` (None: no clip, every part where the file places it), the scene at its
frame 0. The scene's range is the clip's, frames 0 to its duration at the model's fps.
The world box (low, high corners in metres) of every mesh at the scene's current frame.

Import the GLB at ``path`` into the current scene and play ``clip`` (None: stand still). The scene's
frame rate is set to ``fps`` (``render.fps``, with ``render.fps_base`` 1) before the import, which keys
each clip's seconds at it. ``ValueError`` for a file that is no GLB, or one with no node; Blender's own
``RuntimeError`` for one its importer cannot read, once everything the import made is removed.
